items.name: First humans: Happisburgh footprints
facts: Footprints found on the beach at Happisburgh, Norfolk, in 2013 are the oldest known human footprints outside Africa.
They were made at least 850,000 years ago by a small group of adults and children.
The people were probably an extinct human species, perhaps Homo antecessor.
At that time Britain was joined to mainland Europe by land.

items.name: Cheddar Man
facts: Cheddar Man is Britain's oldest almost complete human skeleton, found in Gough's Cave, Somerset, in 1903.
He lived about 10,000 years ago, after the last Ice Age.
He was a hunter-gatherer who lived by hunting, fishing and gathering wild food.
DNA tests in 2018 suggested he probably had dark skin and blue eyes.

items.name: Britain becomes an island
facts: As the ice melted, rising seas slowly flooded Doggerland, the low land joining Britain to Europe.
By about 6500 BC the English Channel and the North Sea had cut Britain off.
Ireland had already been cut off from Britain by the sea thousands of years earlier.

items.name: Farming arrives
facts: Farmers from mainland Europe brought farming to Britain and Ireland around 4000 BC.
They grew wheat and barley and kept cattle, sheep and pigs.
They cleared forests and built long barrows, large earth tombs for their dead.
This period is called the Neolithic, or New Stone Age.

items.name: Newgrange built
facts: Newgrange is a huge passage tomb in the Boyne Valley, County Meath, in Ireland.
It is older than Stonehenge and the Great Pyramid of Giza.
At the winter solstice, sunlight shines along the passage and lights up the inner chamber.

items.name: Skara Brae village
facts: Skara Brae is a Stone Age village on Orkney, off the north coast of Scotland.
Its stone houses still have stone beds, shelves and hearths inside.
People lived there for several hundred years.
A great storm in 1850 uncovered the village from under the sand dunes.

items.name: Stonehenge built
facts: Stonehenge, on Salisbury Plain in Wiltshire, began as a round ditch and bank around 3000 BC.
The giant sarsen stones were put up around 2500 BC.
The smaller bluestones were brought about 150 miles from the Preseli Hills in Wales.
The stones line up with sunrise at midsummer and sunset at midwinter.

items.name: Bronze Age begins
facts: People learned to make bronze by mixing copper with tin.
Copper was mined at places like the Great Orme in Wales, and tin came from Cornwall.
The Amesbury Archer, buried near Stonehenge around 2300 BC, probably grew up in central Europe.
Craftsmen in Ireland made fine gold objects, such as neck collars called lunulae.

items.name: Iron Age and hillforts
facts: Iron tools and weapons spread through Britain and Ireland from about 800 BC.
People built hillforts, such as Maiden Castle in Dorset, with huge earth banks and ditches.
In northern Scotland people built brochs, tall round stone towers.
Most people lived in roundhouses and spoke Celtic languages, the ancestors of Welsh, Cornish and Gaelic.

items.name: Julius Caesar's raids
facts: The Roman general Julius Caesar crossed from Gaul to Britain in 55 BC and again in 54 BC.
In 54 BC he defeated the British leader Cassivellaunus north of the River Thames.
He took hostages and made treaties, but he did not stay to conquer Britain.
He described the Britons in his book about his wars in Gaul.

items.name: Claudius invades Britain
facts: Emperor Claudius sent about 40,000 soldiers, led by Aulus Plautius, to conquer Britain.
They probably landed at Richborough in Kent.
Claudius came himself for about 16 days and entered Camulodunum, now Colchester, with elephants.
Camulodunum became the first capital of Roman Britain.

items.name: Boudica's revolt
facts: Boudica was queen of the Iceni tribe, in what is now Norfolk.
After the Romans flogged her and attacked her daughters, she led a huge revolt.
Her army burned Colchester, London and St Albans while the Roman governor was attacking Anglesey.
She was finally defeated, probably somewhere in the Midlands, and died soon after.

items.name: Agricola and Mons Graupius
facts: Agricola was the Roman governor of Britain from about AD 77 to 84.
He pushed north into Scotland, which the Romans called Caledonia.
At Mons Graupius he defeated the Caledonians, led by Calgacus, but nobody knows exactly where the battle was.
His son-in-law, the historian Tacitus, wrote about his life.

items.name: Hadrian's Wall built
facts: Emperor Hadrian ordered a wall across northern England, starting around AD 122.
It ran about 73 miles from Wallsend on the Tyne to Bowness-on-Solway.
It had forts and small milecastles, and marked the north-west edge of the Roman Empire.
Letters found at nearby Vindolanda fort show the daily lives of soldiers and their families.

items.name: Antonine Wall built
facts: Emperor Antoninus Pius ordered a new wall further north, across central Scotland.
It ran about 39 miles between the Firth of Forth and the River Clyde.
It was made of turf on a stone base, with a deep ditch in front.
The Romans gave it up after about 20 years and went back to Hadrian's Wall.

items.name: Christianity arrives
facts: Christianity reached Roman Britain through traders and soldiers, but exactly when is unknown.
St Alban, a Roman Briton, is said to be Britain's first Christian martyr; his date is uncertain.
Constantine was proclaimed emperor at York in AD 306 and later backed Christianity.
Three bishops from Britain went to a church meeting at Arles, in Gaul, in AD 314.

items.name: Romans leave Britain
facts: Roman troops were taken out of Britain to fight elsewhere in the early 400s.
Around 410, Emperor Honorius is said to have told the British towns to defend themselves.
Picts, Irish raiders and Saxons attacked the unprotected province.
Roman towns, villas and the use of coins soon declined.

items.name: St Patrick in Ireland
facts: Patrick was a Romano-Briton who was captured by Irish raiders as a teenager and kept as a slave.
He escaped, but later went back to Ireland as a Christian missionary.
Tradition says he arrived in 432, but the true dates of his life are uncertain.
He is Ireland's patron saint, and St Patrick's Day is 17 March.

items.name: Anglo-Saxons settle
facts: Angles, Saxons and Jutes from north Germany and Denmark crossed the North Sea to Britain.
They set up kingdoms including Northumbria, Mercia, East Anglia, Wessex and Kent.
Their language, Old English, is the root of modern English.
The Britons held on in the west and north, including Wales, Cornwall and Strathclyde.

items.name: Columba founds Iona
facts: Columba, an Irish monk from a royal family, founded a monastery on the island of Iona in 563.
Monks from Iona spread Christianity among the Picts and into northern England.
Iona became a great centre of learning, and the Book of Kells may have been started there.

items.name: Augustine's mission to Kent
facts: Pope Gregory the Great sent the monk Augustine to convert the Anglo-Saxons.
Augustine landed in Kent and converted King Æthelberht, whose wife Bertha was already Christian.
Augustine became the first Archbishop of Canterbury.

items.name: Sutton Hoo ship burial
facts: A king was buried in a 27-metre ship under a mound at Sutton Hoo, Suffolk.
He was probably Rædwald, King of East Anglia, who died around 624.
The grave was dug up in 1939 by Basil Brown, on land owned by Edith Pretty.
Its treasures, including a famous iron helmet, are in the British Museum.

items.name: Synod of Whitby
facts: King Oswiu of Northumbria called a meeting at Whitby Abbey to settle church disputes.
The main question was how to work out the date of Easter.
Oswiu chose the Roman way over the Irish customs taught by monks from Iona.
This tied the English church more closely to Rome.

items.name: Bede finishes his history
facts: Bede was a monk at Jarrow, in north-east England, and a great scholar.
In 731 he finished his Ecclesiastical History of the English People, written in Latin.
He is called the Father of English History.
He helped make AD dates popular.

items.name: Offa's Dyke built
facts: Offa was a powerful king of Mercia, in the Midlands, who ruled from 757 to 796.
He built a long earth bank and ditch along the border with the Welsh kingdoms.
Parts still stand today, and a long-distance footpath follows its line.
Offa also issued silver pennies, the basis of English money for centuries.

items.name: Vikings raid Lindisfarne
facts: Viking raiders from Scandinavia attacked the monastery on Lindisfarne, off Northumberland, in June 793.
They killed monks and stole treasures, shocking Christian Europe.
Iona was raided soon after, and Vikings later settled in Scotland, Ireland and England.
Vikings founded Dublin as a fortified base in 841.

items.name: Kenneth MacAlpin rules Picts and Scots
facts: Kenneth MacAlpin was king of the Gaelic Scots of Dál Riata, in western Scotland.
Around 843 he also became king of the Picts.
He is traditionally called the first King of Scots.
By about 900 the joint kingdom was called Alba, the Gaelic name for Scotland.

items.name: Great Heathen Army invades
facts: A large Viking army landed in East Anglia in 865.
It captured York in 866, and the Vikings called the city Jorvik.
It conquered Northumbria, East Anglia and much of Mercia.
King Edmund of East Anglia was killed in 869 and later became a saint.

items.name: Alfred wins at Edington
facts: Alfred the Great, King of Wessex, was nearly beaten and hid in the Somerset marshes at Athelney.
In 878 he gathered an army and beat the Viking leader Guthrum at Edington, Wiltshire.
Guthrum became a Christian, and England was split, with the Viking-ruled east called the Danelaw.
Alfred built fortified towns called burhs, and new warships, to defend Wessex.

items.name: Æthelstan unites England
facts: Æthelstan, Alfred's grandson, took York from the Vikings in 927.
This made him the first king to rule all of England.
In 937 he beat an alliance of Scots, Strathclyde Britons and Dublin Vikings at Brunanburh.
Nobody is sure where the Battle of Brunanburh was fought.

items.name: Brian Boru at Clontarf
facts: Brian Boru rose from a small kingdom in Munster to become High King of Ireland.
On Good Friday 1014 his army defeated the men of Leinster and Viking Dublin at Clontarf.
Brian, by then an old man, was killed in his tent during the battle.
Later legend said Clontarf drove the Vikings out of Ireland, which is too simple.

items.name: Cnut becomes king
facts: After years of Viking attacks on Æthelred the Unready, the Danes conquered England.
Cnut, a Danish prince, became King of England in 1016.
He later also ruled Denmark and Norway, creating a North Sea empire.
The story of him ordering back the tide was meant to show that God was greater than kings.

items.name: Battles of Stamford Bridge and Hastings
facts: Edward the Confessor died in January 1066, and Harold Godwinson became king.
On 25 September Harold beat the Norwegian king Harald Hardrada at Stamford Bridge, near York.
On 14 October Duke William of Normandy defeated and killed Harold near Hastings.
William was crowned in Westminster Abbey on Christmas Day 1066.

items.name: Harrying of the North
facts: William crushed rebellions in the north of England, which had Danish support.
His soldiers burned villages, crops and animals across Yorkshire and beyond.
Thousands died of famine; one chronicler claimed 100,000, but historians debate the number.

items.name: Domesday Book
facts: William ordered a great survey of England at Christmas 1085.
It recorded who held land, how many people lived there and what animals they had.
It covered over 13,000 places, but not London, Winchester or most of the far north.
It is kept at the National Archives in Kew.

items.name: Normans invade Ireland
facts: Dermot MacMurrough, the exiled King of Leinster, asked Henry II's lords for help.
Norman knights landed in County Wexford in 1169, and Strongbow took Dublin in 1170.
Henry II came to Ireland himself in 1171 to take control.
It began English rule in Ireland, which lasted in some form for centuries.

items.name: Thomas Becket murdered
facts: Thomas Becket was Archbishop of Canterbury and argued with Henry II about the church's rights.
Four knights killed him in Canterbury Cathedral on 29 December 1170.
They acted after hearing the king's angry words about Becket.
Becket was made a saint in 1173, and Canterbury became a great place of pilgrimage.

items.name: Magna Carta
facts: Rebel barons forced King John to agree to Magna Carta at Runnymede on 15 June 1215.
It said the king must obey the law, and no free man could be jailed without lawful judgement.
The Pope cancelled it within weeks, but it was reissued in 1216, 1217 and 1225.
Four original copies from 1215 still survive.

items.name: Simon de Montfort's Parliament
facts: Simon de Montfort led the barons against Henry III and captured him at Lewes in 1264.
In January 1265 he called a parliament with knights from the counties and men from the towns.
It is seen as an early step towards the House of Commons.
Simon was killed at the Battle of Evesham in August 1265.

items.name: Edward I conquers Wales
facts: Llywelyn ap Gruffudd, the last native Prince of Wales, was killed near Cilmeri in December 1282.
His brother Dafydd was captured and executed in 1283.
Edward built mighty castles at Conwy, Caernarfon, Harlech and Beaumaris.
In 1301 Edward made his son the first English Prince of Wales.

items.name: Wallace wins at Stirling Bridge
facts: Edward I invaded Scotland in 1296 and took the Stone of Destiny to London.
William Wallace and Andrew Moray beat a larger English army at Stirling Bridge on 11 September 1297.
Wallace lost the Battle of Falkirk in 1298.
He was captured and executed in London in 1305.

items.name: Battle of Bannockburn
facts: Robert the Bruce was crowned King of Scots in 1306.
On 23 and 24 June 1314 he defeated Edward II's larger army near Stirling.
It was the greatest Scottish victory of the Wars of Independence.
England finally recognised Scotland's independence in 1328.

items.name: Declaration of Arbroath
facts: Scottish nobles sent a letter to Pope John XXII asking him to accept Scotland's independence.
It said they fought not for glory or riches, but for freedom.
It also said they would get rid of even Robert the Bruce if he gave in to England.

items.name: Hundred Years' War and Crécy
facts: Edward III claimed the French throne, starting a long series of wars with France.
At Crécy in 1346, English and Welsh longbowmen helped defeat a much larger French army.
Edward's son, the Black Prince, fought at Crécy aged 16.
By 1453 England had lost all its French lands except Calais.

items.name: Black Death
facts: The plague arrived at Melcombe, in Dorset, in the summer of 1348.
It killed perhaps a third to a half of the people of Britain and Ireland.
It reached Ireland in 1348 and Scotland in 1349.
With fewer workers left, labourers began to demand higher wages.

items.name: Peasants' Revolt
facts: Anger at a new poll tax led to a rising in Essex and Kent.
Rebels led by Wat Tyler and the priest John Ball marched on London.
The 14-year-old Richard II met them at Smithfield, where Tyler was killed.
The king's promises were broken, and many rebels were executed.

items.name: Owain Glyndŵr's rising
facts: Owain Glyndŵr was proclaimed Prince of Wales in September 1400 and led a revolt against English rule.
He held a Welsh parliament at Machynlleth in 1404.
By 1409 the English had won back his castles at Aberystwyth and Harlech.
He disappeared around 1415 and was never captured.

items.name: Battle of Agincourt
facts: Henry V invaded France to press his claim to the French throne.
On 25 October 1415 his small, tired army beat a much larger French army.
English and Welsh archers and the muddy ground helped win the battle.
In 1420 Henry was named heir to the French king.

items.name: Wars of the Roses
facts: The royal houses of Lancaster and York fought for the English crown.
Their badges included a red rose and a white rose, but the name Wars of the Roses came later.
The Battle of Towton in 1461 is thought to be the bloodiest battle on English soil.
Edward IV's young sons, the Princes in the Tower, vanished in 1483.

items.name: Caxton's printing press
facts: William Caxton set up England's first printing press at Westminster in 1476.
He had learned printing abroad, in Cologne and Bruges.
He printed Chaucer's Canterbury Tales, which had been written in English in the late 1300s.
Printing helped to fix English spelling and spread new ideas.

items.name: Battle of Bosworth
facts: On 22 August 1485 Henry Tudor defeated Richard III near Market Bosworth, Leicestershire.
Henry had Welsh roots and landed at Milford Haven, gathering Welsh support as he marched.
Richard III was the last English king to die in battle.
His skeleton was found under a car park in Leicester in 2012.

items.name: Battle of Flodden
facts: James IV of Scotland invaded England while Henry VIII was fighting in France.
On 9 September 1513 the English defeated the Scots at Flodden, in Northumberland.
James IV and many Scottish nobles were killed.
He was the last monarch in Britain to die in battle.

items.name: Henry VIII breaks with Rome
facts: Henry wanted to end his marriage to Catherine of Aragon, who had not given him a son.
When the Pope refused, Henry made himself head of the Church in England by the Act of Supremacy.
He married Anne Boleyn in 1533, and their daughter became Elizabeth I.
Henry married six times in all.

items.name: Laws in Wales Acts
facts: These laws joined Wales to England in law and government.
Wales was divided into counties and sent MPs to Parliament in London.
English became the language of the law and official business in Wales.

items.name: Dissolution of the Monasteries
facts: Thomas Cromwell, Henry VIII's minister, closed about 800 monasteries, abbeys and nunneries.
Their land and riches went to the Crown and were sold to nobles and gentry.
The Pilgrimage of Grace, a large rising in northern England in 1536, was crushed.
Ruins such as Fountains Abbey and Tintern Abbey date from this time.

items.name: Mary, Queen of Scots executed
facts: Mary became Queen of Scots in 1542, when she was six days old.
Scotland became Protestant in 1560, but Mary stayed Catholic.
She was forced to give up her throne in 1567 and fled to England.
After 19 years as a prisoner, she was executed at Fotheringhay Castle for plotting against Elizabeth I.

items.name: Spanish Armada
facts: Philip II of Spain sent about 130 ships to invade Protestant England.
Elizabeth I made a famous speech to her troops at Tilbury.
English fireships broke up the Spanish fleet off Calais.
Storms wrecked many Spanish ships on the coasts of Scotland and Ireland as they sailed home.

items.name: Shakespeare's plays
facts: William Shakespeare was born in Stratford-upon-Avon in 1564 and died in 1616.
He wrote around 37 plays and 154 sonnets.
Many of his plays were performed at the Globe Theatre in London, built in 1599.
His friends published his plays in the First Folio in 1623.

items.name: Union of the Crowns
facts: Elizabeth I died in 1603 without children.
Her relative James VI of Scotland became James I of England and Ireland.
England and Scotland now shared a king, but kept separate parliaments and laws.
James ordered a new English Bible, the King James Bible, published in 1611.

items.name: Gunpowder Plot
facts: Catholic plotters led by Robert Catesby planned to blow up Parliament and King James.
Guy Fawkes was caught guarding barrels of gunpowder under the House of Lords on the night of 4 November.
The plotters were killed or executed.
Bonfire Night on 5 November remembers the failure of the plot.

items.name: Plantation of Ulster
facts: Irish lords led by Hugh O'Neill lost the Nine Years' War in 1603 and fled abroad in 1607.
The Crown took their land in Ulster and gave it to Protestant settlers from Scotland and England.
New towns were built, including Londonderry, paid for by London companies.
The divide between settlers and native Irish shaped Ulster's later conflicts.

items.name: Civil Wars
facts: Charles I quarrelled with Parliament over money, power and religion.
Fighting also took place in Scotland and Ireland, so they are called the Wars of the Three Kingdoms.
Royalists, or Cavaliers, fought Parliamentarians, or Roundheads.
Parliament's New Model Army won a decisive victory at Naseby in 1645.

items.name: Charles I executed
facts: Parliament put Charles I on trial for treason.
He was beheaded outside the Banqueting House in Whitehall on 30 January 1649.
England became a republic, called the Commonwealth.
Oliver Cromwell ruled as Lord Protector from 1653 until his death in 1658.

items.name: Cromwell in Ireland
facts: Cromwell led an army to Ireland in 1649 to crush Royalists and Catholic rebels.
His troops killed thousands, including civilians, at Drogheda and Wexford.
Much Catholic-owned land was taken and given to soldiers and Protestant settlers.
Cromwell is still remembered with bitterness in Ireland.

items.name: Restoration of the monarchy
facts: After Cromwell died, Parliament invited Charles I's son back from exile.
Charles II entered London on 29 May 1660, his 30th birthday.
Theatres reopened, and the Royal Society for science was founded in 1660.
Cromwell's body was dug up, and his head was put on a pole.

items.name: Great Plague of London
facts: Bubonic plague killed about 100,000 people in London, around a quarter of its people.
It was probably spread by fleas carried by rats.
The rich, including the king, fled the city.
The village of Eyam, in Derbyshire, cut itself off to stop the plague spreading.

items.name: Great Fire of London
facts: The fire started in a baker's shop on Pudding Lane on 2 September 1666.
It burned for four days and destroyed about 13,000 houses and old St Paul's Cathedral.
Only a few deaths were recorded, but the true number is unknown.
Christopher Wren designed the new St Paul's and many City churches.

items.name: Glorious Revolution
facts: Many feared that the Catholic James II would make England Catholic again.
His Protestant daughter Mary and her Dutch husband, William of Orange, were invited to take the throne.
William landed in Devon in November 1688, and James fled to France.
The Bill of Rights of 1689 limited the monarch's power and gave Parliament more control.

items.name: Battle of the Boyne
facts: James II tried to win back his throne from Ireland, with French support.
In 1689 Protestant Derry held out against James's army in a siege of 105 days.
William III defeated James at the River Boyne on 1 July 1690.
Orange marches in Northern Ireland on 12 July still mark the victory.

items.name: Massacre of Glencoe
facts: Highland chiefs were told to swear loyalty to William III by 1 January 1692.
Alasdair MacIain, chief of the MacDonalds of Glencoe, swore his oath a few days late.
On 13 February, government soldiers who had been their guests killed 38 MacDonalds.
Others died of cold after fleeing into the snow.

items.name: Act of Union
facts: England and Scotland joined to form the Kingdom of Great Britain on 1 May 1707.
The Scottish Parliament closed, and Scottish MPs went to Westminster.
Scotland kept its own law, church and schools.
Money troubles after Scotland's failed colony at Darien, in Panama, helped push it towards union.

items.name: Jacobite risings and Culloden
facts: Jacobites wanted to bring back the Catholic Stuarts, descendants of James II, to the throne.
The 1715 rising, led by the Earl of Mar, failed after the Battle of Sheriffmuir.
In 1745 Bonnie Prince Charlie raised an army in the Highlands and marched as far as Derby.
His army was crushed at Culloden, near Inverness, on 16 April 1746, the last pitched battle on British soil.

items.name: Walpole, the first Prime Minister
facts: George I, from Hanover in Germany, became king in 1714.
Robert Walpole led the government from 1721 to 1742 and is seen as the first Prime Minister.
The title Prime Minister was not official at the time.
Walpole moved into 10 Downing Street in 1735.

items.name: Seven Years' War
facts: Britain fought France and its allies in Europe, North America and India.
Robert Clive's victory at Plassey in 1757 helped the East India Company take control of Bengal.
General Wolfe captured Quebec in 1759 but was killed in the battle.
Britain won Canada and became the leading colonial power.

items.name: Industrial Revolution
facts: Britain became the first country to industrialise, using coal, iron and steam power.
James Watt, a Scottish engineer, greatly improved the steam engine from 1769.
Richard Arkwright's water-powered cotton mill at Cromford opened in 1771.
People moved from the countryside to fast-growing towns like Manchester, Glasgow and Merthyr Tydfil.

items.name: Captain Cook's voyages
facts: James Cook led three great voyages of exploration in the Pacific Ocean.
In 1770 he mapped the east coast of Australia and claimed it for Britain.
He also mapped New Zealand and sailed far south towards Antarctica.
He was killed in Hawaii in 1779.

items.name: Loss of the American colonies
facts: Thirteen American colonies rebelled against British taxes and rule.
They declared independence on 4 July 1776.
A British army surrendered at Yorktown in 1781, after France joined the Americans.
Britain recognised the United States in the Treaty of Paris in 1783.

items.name: Irish rebellion
facts: The United Irishmen, led by Wolfe Tone, wanted an independent Irish republic.
Their members included both Catholics and Protestants.
The rising was crushed, with thousands killed, including at Vinegar Hill in County Wexford.
A small French force landed in County Mayo but was defeated.

items.name: Act of Union with Ireland
facts: The United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland was created on 1 January 1801.
The Irish Parliament in Dublin was closed, and Irish MPs went to Westminster.
The red cross of St Patrick was added to the Union Flag.
Promised rights for Catholics were not given, and Prime Minister Pitt the Younger resigned.

items.name: Battle of Trafalgar
facts: On 21 October 1805 Admiral Nelson's fleet defeated the French and Spanish fleets off Spain.
Nelson was shot and killed during the battle.
The victory ended Napoleon's hopes of invading Britain.
Nelson's Column in Trafalgar Square, London, remembers him.

items.name: Slave trade abolished
facts: From 1787, campaigners such as Thomas Clarkson and Olaudah Equiano fought to end the slave trade.
William Wilberforce led the campaign in Parliament for many years.
Ordinary people signed petitions and refused to buy sugar grown by enslaved people.
The 1807 Act banned British ships from carrying enslaved Africans, but slavery itself continued.

items.name: Battle of Waterloo
facts: Napoleon escaped from exile and returned to power in France in 1815.
On 18 June 1815 the Duke of Wellington and the Prussian general Blücher defeated him near Brussels.
Napoleon was sent to the remote island of St Helena, where he died in 1821.
It ended over 20 years of war between Britain and France.

items.name: Peterloo Massacre
facts: Around 60,000 people gathered at St Peter's Field, Manchester, to call for the vote.
Soldiers on horseback charged the crowd with sabres.
About 18 people were killed and hundreds were injured.
The name Peterloo mocked the Battle of Waterloo.

items.name: Stockton and Darlington Railway
facts: It opened on 27 September 1825 in north-east England.
It was the world's first public railway to use steam locomotives.
George Stephenson's engine Locomotion No. 1 pulled the first train.
The Liverpool and Manchester Railway, opened in 1830, was the first inter-city line.

items.name: Catholic Emancipation
facts: Catholics had long been banned from sitting in Parliament.
The Irish leader Daniel O'Connell won an election in County Clare in 1828 but could not take his seat.
Fearing unrest in Ireland, the Duke of Wellington's government let Catholics become MPs in 1829.
O'Connell became known as the Liberator.

items.name: Great Reform Act
facts: Many new industrial towns, such as Manchester, had no MPs of their own.
Rotten boroughs with almost no voters, like Old Sarum, still elected MPs.
The Act gave seats to big towns and let more middle-class men vote.
Still only about one in five adult men in England and Wales could vote.

items.name: Slavery Abolition Act
facts: The Act ended slavery in most of the British Empire from 1 August 1834.
Slave owners were paid £20 million in compensation, but enslaved people got nothing.
Most freed people were made to keep working for their old owners until 1838.

items.name: Victoria becomes queen
facts: Victoria became queen on 20 June 1837, aged 18.
In 1840 she married her German cousin, Prince Albert.
She reigned for 63 years, longer than any monarch before her.
Her nine children married into royal families across Europe.

items.name: Chartists
facts: The People's Charter of 1838 called for votes for all men and secret ballots.
Millions signed huge petitions, but Parliament rejected them.
In the Newport Rising of 1839, in Wales, soldiers killed over 20 Chartists.
Most of the Charter's demands became law later.

items.name: Penny post
facts: Rowland Hill proposed a cheap postal service with one price for any distance.
The Penny Black, the world's first postage stamp, was issued in May 1840.
Senders now paid for letters, instead of the person receiving them.

items.name: Great Famine in Ireland
facts: A disease called potato blight destroyed the potatoes that most poor Irish families lived on.
About one million people died from hunger and disease.
More than a million others emigrated, many to America, Britain and Canada.
Food was still exported from Ireland, and the government's response is still criticised.

items.name: Corn Laws repealed
facts: The Corn Laws taxed imported grain, keeping bread prices high.
The Anti-Corn Law League, led by Richard Cobden and John Bright, campaigned for free trade.
Prime Minister Robert Peel repealed the laws, partly because of the Irish famine.
This split his Conservative Party.

items.name: Great Exhibition
facts: It was held in the Crystal Palace, a huge glass building in Hyde Park, London.
Prince Albert helped organise it to show off industry from around the world.
There were about six million visits.
Its profits helped to build the museums in South Kensington.

items.name: Crimean War and Florence Nightingale
facts: Britain, France and the Ottoman Empire fought Russia, mainly in Crimea on the Black Sea.
The Charge of the Light Brigade at Balaclava in 1854 was a famous blunder.
Florence Nightingale improved hospital care for wounded soldiers at Scutari, in Turkey.
Mary Seacole, a Jamaican nurse, ran a hotel for soldiers near the front.

items.name: Indian Rebellion and the Raj
facts: Indian soldiers in the East India Company's army rebelled at Meerut in 1857.
The fighting was brutal on both sides, and the rebellion was crushed in 1858.
The British government then took over from the Company; its rule was called the Raj.
Victoria was made Empress of India in 1876.

items.name: Darwin's Origin of Species
facts: Charles Darwin sailed round the world on HMS Beagle from 1831 to 1836.
His book On the Origin of Species explained evolution by natural selection.
Alfred Russel Wallace, born in Monmouthshire, came up with the same idea.
Their ideas caused fierce debate with some religious leaders.

items.name: Second Reform Act
facts: Benjamin Disraeli's Conservative government passed the Act.
It gave the vote to many working men in towns, roughly doubling the number of voters.
Secret ballots for elections began in 1872.
The Third Reform Act of 1884 gave many men in the countryside the vote.

items.name: Education Act
facts: The Act set up board schools wherever there were not enough church schools in England and Wales.
Scotland passed a similar act in 1872.
School became compulsory for young children in 1880, and mostly free in 1891.

items.name: Scramble for Africa
facts: European powers rushed to take control of almost all of Africa.
The Berlin Conference of 1884 to 1885 set rules for dividing up the continent.
Britain took large areas, including Egypt, Nigeria, Kenya and much of southern Africa.
By 1914 the British Empire ruled around a quarter of the world's people.

items.name: Irish Home Rule crisis
facts: Home Rule meant a parliament in Dublin to run Irish affairs.
Charles Stewart Parnell led the Irish Party at Westminster and fought for tenant farmers' rights.
Gladstone's first Home Rule Bill was defeated in 1886, splitting his Liberal Party.
His second Bill passed the Commons in 1893 but was blocked by the House of Lords.

items.name: Boer War
facts: Britain fought the Boers, settlers of Dutch descent in southern Africa, partly over gold.
The Boers besieged British forces in towns such as Mafeking, which was relieved in 1900.
The British put Boer and Black African civilians in concentration camps, where many thousands died.
Britain won, and the Boer republics became part of the Empire.

items.name: Queen Victoria dies
facts: Victoria died on 22 January 1901 at Osborne House on the Isle of Wight.
Her son became King Edward VII.
Her reign of 63 years was the longest until Elizabeth II.

items.name: Suffragettes
facts: Emmeline Pankhurst founded the Women's Social and Political Union in Manchester in 1903.
Their motto was deeds not words, and they smashed windows and started fires.
Suffragettes in prison went on hunger strike and were force-fed.
Emily Davison died after running in front of the king's horse at the 1913 Derby.

items.name: Liberal reforms and People's Budget
facts: The Liberal government let councils give free school meals to poor children from 1906.
Old age pensions began in 1908, paying up to five shillings a week to people over 70.
The House of Lords rejected Lloyd George's People's Budget, which taxed the rich, in 1909.
The Parliament Act 1911 meant the Lords could only delay most laws, not block them.

items.name: Titanic sinks
facts: The Titanic was built at Harland and Wolff's shipyard in Belfast.
It hit an iceberg on its first voyage and sank on 15 April 1912.
About 1,500 people died, partly because there were not enough lifeboats.

items.name: First World War
facts: Britain declared war on Germany on 4 August 1914, after Germany invaded Belgium.
On 1 July 1916, the first day of the Battle of the Somme, about 19,000 British soldiers were killed.
Around 880,000 British servicemen died in the war.
The war ended with the Armistice at 11am on 11 November 1918.

items.name: Easter Rising
facts: On Easter Monday, 24 April 1916, Irish rebels seized buildings in Dublin, including the General Post Office.
Patrick Pearse read out a proclamation of an Irish Republic.
The rising was crushed within a week.
The execution of its leaders turned many Irish people towards independence.

items.name: Votes for women
facts: In 1918 many women over 30, and all men over 21, got the vote.
Constance Markievicz was the first woman elected as an MP, in 1918, but as a Sinn Féin MP she refused to sit.
Nancy Astor became the first woman to sit as an MP, in 1919.
In 1928 women got the vote on the same terms as men, from age 21.

items.name: Irish independence and partition
facts: Sinn Féin MPs set up their own parliament, the Dáil, in Dublin in January 1919.
The IRA, with Michael Collins, fought British forces in the War of Independence.
In 1921 six north-eastern counties became Northern Ireland, staying in the UK.
The Anglo-Irish Treaty created the Irish Free State in 1922, and a bitter civil war followed.

items.name: BBC founded
facts: The British Broadcasting Company was set up in October 1922 and began radio broadcasts in November.
It became the British Broadcasting Corporation, a public body, in 1927.
Its first leader, John Reith, said it should inform, educate and entertain.
It started the world's first regular high-definition television service in 1936.

items.name: General Strike
facts: Mine owners wanted to cut miners' wages and make them work longer hours.
The TUC called a general strike, and about 1.7 million workers stopped work.
It lasted nine days, from 4 to 12 May 1926.
The miners stayed out for months but were forced back on worse terms.

items.name: Depression and Jarrow March
facts: The Great Depression after 1929 caused mass unemployment, worst in industrial areas.
In Jarrow, near Newcastle, most men were out of work after Palmer's shipyard closed.
In October 1936 about 200 men marched nearly 300 miles to London with a petition.
The march became a symbol of the hungry thirties.

items.name: Abdication of Edward VIII
facts: Edward VIII wanted to marry Wallis Simpson, an American who had been divorced twice.
The government and the Church of England would not accept the marriage.
He gave up the throne on 11 December 1936, after less than a year as king.
His brother became King George VI.

items.name: Second World War
facts: Britain declared war on Germany on 3 September 1939, after Germany invaded Poland.
Winston Churchill became Prime Minister in May 1940.
Code-breakers at Bletchley Park cracked German codes, including Enigma messages.
About 450,000 people from the UK died, including around 70,000 civilians.

items.name: Dunkirk evacuation
facts: German forces trapped the British army on the French coast in May 1940.
About 338,000 British and French soldiers were rescued between 26 May and 4 June.
Hundreds of small civilian boats helped the Royal Navy.
Churchill called it a miracle but warned that wars are not won by evacuations.

items.name: Battle of Britain
facts: From July to October 1940 the RAF fought the German air force over southern England.
Germany needed control of the air before it could invade.
Radar and fighter planes like the Spitfire and Hurricane were vital.
Churchill said never was so much owed by so many to so few.

items.name: The Blitz
facts: German bombers attacked British cities from September 1940 to May 1941.
London was bombed on 57 nights in a row.
Coventry, Liverpool, Clydebank, Belfast, Swansea and many other places were badly hit.
About 43,000 civilians were killed.

items.name: D-Day landings
facts: On 6 June 1944 Allied forces landed on five beaches in Normandy, France.
British troops landed on Gold and Sword beaches, and Canadians on Juno.
About 156,000 soldiers landed on the first day.
It began the freeing of western Europe from Nazi rule.

items.name: VE Day
facts: Germany surrendered, and 8 May 1945 was celebrated as Victory in Europe Day.
Huge crowds filled London, and Churchill joined the royal family on the Buckingham Palace balcony.
The war with Japan ended in August 1945, after atomic bombs were dropped on Hiroshima and Nagasaki.

items.name: Attlee's Labour landslide
facts: Labour, led by Clement Attlee, won a landslide in July 1945, defeating Churchill.
It followed the 1942 Beveridge Report, which aimed to defeat want, disease, ignorance, squalor and idleness.
Labour took coal, the railways and other industries into public ownership.
It built the welfare state, including family allowances and national insurance.

items.name: Indian independence
facts: India and Pakistan became independent on 15 August 1947.
British India was partitioned, mainly along religious lines.
Violence during partition killed hundreds of thousands, and millions had to leave their homes.
Burma and Ceylon, now Sri Lanka, became independent in 1948.

items.name: Empire Windrush arrives
facts: The ship Empire Windrush arrived at Tilbury, Essex, on 22 June 1948.
It carried hundreds of people from the Caribbean who came to work and help rebuild Britain.
People who came from the Caribbean in these years are called the Windrush generation.
In 2018 a scandal showed some had been wrongly told they had no right to live in Britain.

items.name: NHS founded
facts: The National Health Service began on 5 July 1948.
Aneurin Bevan, the health minister, from Tredegar in Wales, set it up.
For the first time, healthcare was free for everyone when they used it.
Similar health services were set up in Scotland and Northern Ireland.

items.name: Coronation of Elizabeth II
facts: Elizabeth became queen on 6 February 1952, when her father, George VI, died.
She was crowned in Westminster Abbey on 2 June 1953.
Millions watched on television, and many families bought their first set for it.
News that a British-led team had climbed Everest arrived on the same day.

items.name: Suez Crisis
facts: Egypt's leader, Nasser, took over the Suez Canal, which was run by a British and French company.
Britain, France and Israel secretly planned an attack on Egypt.
The USA forced them to withdraw, a great humiliation for Britain.
Prime Minister Anthony Eden resigned in January 1957.

items.name: End of empire
facts: Ghana, in 1957, was among the first British colonies in Africa to become independent.
In 1960 Harold Macmillan said a wind of change was blowing through Africa.
Kenya became independent in 1963, after the violent Mau Mau uprising.
Most former colonies joined the Commonwealth.

items.name: Swinging Sixties and the Beatles
facts: The Beatles, from Liverpool, released their first single, Love Me Do, in 1962.
Beatlemania swept Britain and then the USA.
London became a centre of fashion, with Mary Quant's miniskirts and Carnaby Street.
New laws ended hanging for murder in 1965 and partly decriminalised sex between men in 1967.

items.name: England win the World Cup
facts: England hosted the football World Cup in 1966.
They beat West Germany 4–2 after extra time in the final at Wembley on 30 July.
Geoff Hurst scored a hat-trick, and Bobby Moore was captain.

items.name: Aberfan disaster
facts: On 21 October 1966 a coal waste tip slid down onto the village of Aberfan, in South Wales.
It buried Pantglas Junior School and nearby houses.
144 people were killed, 116 of them children.
An inquiry blamed the National Coal Board.

items.name: The Troubles and Bloody Sunday
facts: In Northern Ireland, Catholic civil rights marchers protested against unfair treatment in housing, jobs and voting.
British troops were sent onto the streets in August 1969.
On Bloody Sunday, 30 January 1972, soldiers shot dead 13 civil rights marchers in Derry; another died later.
Over 3,500 people were killed by republicans, loyalists and the security forces.

items.name: Britain joins the EEC
facts: Britain joined the European Economic Community on 1 January 1973, along with Ireland and Denmark.
Edward Heath's Conservative government took Britain in.
France's President de Gaulle had blocked earlier British attempts to join in 1963 and 1967.
In a 1975 referendum, about two-thirds voted to stay in.

items.name: Thatcher becomes Prime Minister
facts: Margaret Thatcher became Britain's first woman Prime Minister on 4 May 1979.
She won after the Winter of Discontent, when many public workers went on strike.
She sold off state-owned industries and let council tenants buy their homes.
Her unpopular poll tax helped to bring her down in 1990.

items.name: Falklands War
facts: Argentina invaded the Falkland Islands, a British territory in the South Atlantic, on 2 April 1982.
Britain sent a naval task force about 8,000 miles south.
Argentine forces surrendered on 14 June 1982.
255 British service personnel, 649 Argentines and three islanders died.

items.name: Miners' strike
facts: Miners went on strike against pit closures, led by Arthur Scargill of the National Union of Mineworkers.
There were violent clashes with police, such as at Orgreave in South Yorkshire.
The strike lasted about a year and ended in defeat for the miners.
Most coal mines closed over the next ten years, hitting communities in Wales, Scotland and northern England.

items.name: Channel Tunnel opens
facts: The Queen and French President Mitterrand opened the tunnel on 6 May 1994.
It runs about 31 miles between Folkestone and Calais, much of it under the sea.
It is the first fixed link between Britain and mainland Europe since Britain became an island.
Eurostar trains link London with Paris and Brussels.

items.name: Devolution for Scotland and Wales
facts: Tony Blair's Labour Party won a landslide in May 1997.
In September 1997 Scotland voted strongly for its own parliament, and Wales narrowly voted for an assembly.
The Scottish Parliament and the National Assembly for Wales opened in 1999.
Donald Dewar became Scotland's first First Minister.

items.name: Good Friday Agreement
facts: The agreement was signed in Belfast on 10 April 1998, which was Good Friday.
It set up a power-sharing government in Northern Ireland for unionists and nationalists.
Voters in Northern Ireland and the Republic of Ireland approved it in May 1998.
It said Northern Ireland would stay in the UK unless a majority there voted to leave.

items.name: Iraq War
facts: Britain joined the USA in invading Iraq in March 2003.
Hundreds of thousands of people marched against the war in London in February 2003.
No weapons of mass destruction were found.
179 British service personnel died, and the 2016 Chilcot report criticised the decision to go to war.

items.name: 7/7 London bombings
facts: On 7 July 2005 four suicide bombers attacked three Tube trains and a bus in London.
52 people were killed and hundreds were injured.
It happened the day after London was chosen to host the 2012 Olympics.

items.name: Financial crisis
facts: In 2007 savers queued to take their money out of Northern Rock, the first run on a British bank in over a century.
In 2008 the government rescued big banks, including RBS and Lloyds.
Britain fell into recession, and years of spending cuts followed.
In 2010 the Conservatives and Liberal Democrats formed the first coalition government since the war.

items.name: London Olympics
facts: London hosted the Olympic Games from 27 July to 12 August 2012.
Danny Boyle's opening ceremony showed British history, from farms and factories to the NHS.
Team GB won 29 gold medals and came third in the medal table.
London became the first city to host the modern summer Olympics three times.

items.name: Scottish independence referendum
facts: On 18 September 2014 Scotland voted on whether to become an independent country.
No won by 55% to 45%.
Turnout was about 85%, and 16 and 17-year-olds could vote.

items.name: Brexit referendum
facts: On 23 June 2016 the UK voted to leave the European Union by 52% to 48%.
England and Wales voted to leave, but Scotland and Northern Ireland voted to remain.
David Cameron announced his resignation the next day, and Theresa May became Prime Minister.

items.name: Grenfell Tower fire
facts: On 14 June 2017 fire spread through Grenfell Tower, a block of flats in west London.
72 people died.
Flammable cladding on the outside of the building helped the fire spread.
A public inquiry found that all the deaths could have been avoided.

items.name: UK leaves the EU
facts: Boris Johnson won a big majority in December 2019, promising to get Brexit done.
The UK left the EU at 11pm on 31 January 2020.
A transition period ended on 31 December 2020.
Northern Ireland has special trade rules to avoid a hard border with Ireland.

items.name: Covid-19 pandemic
facts: The first national lockdown began on 23 March 2020.
On 8 December 2020 Margaret Keenan, in Coventry, was the first person in the world given an approved Covid vaccine.
Over 200,000 people in the UK died with Covid on their death certificate.
Parties held in Downing Street during lockdown led to the Partygate scandal.

items.name: Death of Elizabeth II
facts: Elizabeth II died at Balmoral, in Scotland, on 8 September 2022, aged 96.
She had reigned for 70 years, longer than any other British monarch.
Two days before she died, she appointed Liz Truss, her 15th Prime Minister.
Her son became King Charles III and was crowned on 6 May 2023.

items.name: Labour landslide
facts: Labour, led by Keir Starmer, won the general election on 4 July 2024.
Labour won 411 seats, and the Conservatives fell to 121, their worst result ever.
The Liberal Democrats and Reform UK also made big gains.
It ended 14 years of Conservative government.

items.name: Burnham becomes Prime Minister
facts: Andy Burnham, the Mayor of Greater Manchester, won the Makerfield by-election held on 18 June 2026.
Keir Starmer announced his resignation on 22 June 2026, after pressure from within Labour.
Burnham was elected Labour leader unopposed on 17 July 2026.
He became Prime Minister on 20 July 2026.
